en: Wealthy; having a lot of money
hook: AFFLUENT: money FLOWS in (fluent).
story: Affluent. Lamia's school friend lived in Gulshan, in a house with a swimming pool, three cars, and a cook who made whatever she wanted. Lamia's own family shared a two room flat in Mirpur. Her friend's family was affluent: wealthy, having plenty of money. Affluent comes from the Latin for flowing toward, as if money flows in like a river. Affluence means wealth, and an affluent suburb is a rich one. Its opposite is impoverished. Synonyms: wealthy, prosperous, well off.

gre.s: Although the town was once ____, sustained by a booming textile trade, it sank into poverty when the mills closed and its young people moved away.
gre.clue: sustained by a booming textile trade

example: As the suburb grew more affluent, its small tailoring shops gave way to boutiques selling imported clothes.

en: Covering every part or aspect, leaving nothing out
hook: ALL-ENCOMPASSING: a COMPASS that circles everything.
story: All-encompassing. When Rafi's grandfather began writing a history of their village, he did not stop at the important families. He recorded every pond, every mosque and temple, every flood since 1950, even the names of cows and the recipes for festival sweets. His notebook was all-encompassing: including absolutely everything. To encompass is to surround or include, as if drawing a circle with a compass around it all. An all-encompassing grief fills every corner of life. Synonyms: comprehensive, exhaustive, universal.

gre.s: Far from the narrow survey its modest title suggested, the study was nearly ____, covering every aspect of the region's economy from river fishing to software.
gre.clue: covering every aspect of the region's economy

example: Her grief after the accident was all-encompassing, colouring every meal, every conversation and every song she heard on the radio.

en: Similar or comparable in some way
hook: ANALOGOUS: makes an ANALOGY possible.
story: Analogous. The biology students were lost. The teacher tried again: "Think of the heart as a water pump. Both push liquid through a system of pipes. Both have valves that stop backflow. Both fail if the pipes get blocked." Suddenly, every face lit up. The heart is analogous to a pump: comparable to it in certain important ways. Analogous means similar enough to allow a useful comparison. GRE analogies depend on spotting analogous relationships.

gre.s: The author argues that the decline of the empire is ____ to the collapse of a modern corporation, since both were undone by overexpansion and internal rivalry.
gre.clue: since both were undone by overexpansion and internal rivalry

example: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are analogous structures, since both allow flight but they evolved entirely separately.

en: Very old or old-fashioned; no longer in everyday use
hook: ARCHAIC: as old as ARCHAEOLOGY digs.
story: Archaic. Nadia's grandmother still writes letters the way she learned in 1962: "Henceforth, I beseech thee to partake of thy meals in a timely fashion." Her grandchildren giggle and read them aloud in dramatic voices. To modern ears the language sounds archaic: very old-fashioned, belonging to an earlier period and no longer in everyday use. Some laws are archaic too, written for a world that no longer exists. Think: as old as an archaeology dig.

gre.s: Although the statute remains on the books, it is so ____ that no court has enforced it in over a century.
gre.clue: no court has enforced it in over a century

example: Several archaic words, such as thou and hath, survive in the old hymns the choir still sings each Christmas.

en: Excessively complicated and involving many confusing details, especially bureaucracy
hook: BYZANTINE: like the ancient Byzantine Empire's maze-like bureaucracy.
story: Byzantine. To get a simple trade license, Kamal needed eleven forms, seven offices, four signatures, two stamps, and a mysterious "approval from upstairs" that nobody could explain. Each office sent him to another office. After three months, he was back where he began. The process was byzantine: excessively complicated, full of confusing details and devious procedures. The word recalls the Byzantine Empire, famous for its maze-like bureaucracy and palace intrigue.

gre.s: The tax code has become so ____ that even professional accountants struggle to navigate its thousands of overlapping rules and exceptions.
gre.clue: thousands of overlapping rules and exceptions

example: Getting a refund from the airline involved a byzantine process of forms, phone calls and emails that dragged on for nearly six months.

en: To examine and remove objectionable parts from media
hook: CENSOR: CUTS out what's forbidden. Not censure (criticize).
story: Censor. Under a military government, a newspaper editor had to send his pages to a government office every night. Officers read each article and cut any line that criticised the rulers. Some mornings, the paper appeared with blank white columns. The officers were censoring the news: examining it and removing parts they considered objectionable. A censor is also the person who does this. Do not confuse censor with censure, which means to criticise harshly. Synonyms: suppress, redact, expurgate.

gre.s: Rather than ____ the novel's explicit passages, as the publisher had demanded, the author withdrew the manuscript entirely, insisting that every word remain intact.
gre.clue: insisting that every word remain intact

example: Wartime officials censored soldiers' letters home, blacking out any mention of where the troops were stationed.

en: Standing out clearly; easy to notice
hook: CON-SPIC-uous: SPIC sounds like 'spec', as in spectacle. Everyone can see it.
story: Conspicuous. Everyone at the wedding wore soft pastel colours. Then Arif walked in wearing a bright orange suit. Heads turned. Aunties whispered. The photographer kept pointing his camera at him by mistake. Even the bride glanced over twice. Arif simply could not be missed. Conspicuous means standing out so clearly that everyone notices. If you want to be conspicuous, wear orange to a pastel wedding. If you want to be inconspicuous, wear beige and stand near the snacks.

gre.s: The detective was puzzled that the thief had chosen such a ____ getaway car, a bright yellow convertible that half the town would remember.
gre.clue: half the town would remember

example: As the only tall tree among the paddy fields, the old palm is conspicuous from miles away and guides travelers to the village.

en: Familiar with and at ease in many different countries and cultures
hook: COSMOS = world, POLIS = city. A citizen of the world.
story: Cosmopolitan. Mitu's aunt has lived in London, Tokyo, Nairobi, and Toronto. She speaks four languages, cooks dishes from twelve countries, and has friends on every continent. At a party she moves easily from a Japanese businessman to a Kenyan artist to a Bangladeshi grandmother, at home with everyone. She is truly cosmopolitan: worldly, sophisticated, and comfortable with many cultures. Cosmos means world, polis means city. A citizen of the world.

gre.s: The port's ____ character, shaped by centuries of traders from dozens of nations, contrasted sharply with the insular villages of the interior.
gre.clue: contrasted sharply with the insular villages

example: Chattogram has long been a cosmopolitan port, where Arab, Portuguese and Burmese traders once mingled along the banks of the Karnaphuli.

en: A mistaken belief that someone clings to in spite of clear proof
hook: DELUSION: an ILLUSION you won't let go of.
story: Delusion. Tareq failed his practice tests month after month, never opened his vocabulary list, and skipped every mock exam. Yet he told everyone he would score in the top one percent because he was naturally smart. His friends warned him; he laughed. He was living under a delusion: a false belief held firmly despite evidence against it. Delusions of grandeur are fantasies about one's own greatness. Compare illusion, a false perception of the senses. Synonyms: fantasy, misconception, self-deception.

gre.s: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt, the founder clung to the ____ that a single blockbuster product would restore its fortunes.
gre.clue: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt

example: Many smokers cling to the delusion that they can quit whenever they like, long after the habit has taken hold.

en: A follower of a teacher, leader, or philosophy
hook: DISCIPLE: follows the DISCIPLINE of a master.
story: Disciple. Every evening, a group of young singers sat cross-legged on the floor of an old house in Kushtia, learning Lalon songs from an elderly master. They copied his breathing, his gestures, even the way he tilted his head. Years later, one of them became famous, and in every interview he called himself the master's disciple: a devoted follower of a teacher, leader, or philosophy. Disciple shares a root with discipline; both come from learning. Synonyms: follower, devotee, adherent.

gre.s: Far from rejecting his mentor's theories, the young economist proved to be her most faithful ____, defending her ideas long after the rest of the profession had abandoned them.
gre.clue: defending her ideas long after the rest of the profession had abandoned them

example: As a young disciple of the sitar master, Nazmul spent years practising scales before he was allowed to perform in public.

en: Spreading apart; different from each other
hook: DI-VERGE: two paths going different ways.
story: Divergent. Twin brothers Arif and Asif grew up in the same house, went to the same school, and loved the same cricket team. But at eighteen, their paths split. Arif became a monk in a Buddhist monastery in Bandarban. Asif became a stockbroker in Singapore. Their lives could not be more divergent: moving apart in different directions. Divergent opinions are views that disagree. Its opposite is convergent, meaning coming together.

gre.s: The two economists' forecasts are sharply ____, one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession.
gre.clue: one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession

example: Raised in the same house, the two cousins held sharply divergent views on almost every political question of the day.

en: Picking freely from many different sources or styles
hook: ECLECTIC: ELECTS a bit from everywhere.
story: Eclectic. Joya's playlist confuses her friends. Rabindra Sangeet is followed by Korean pop, then a Bach cello suite, then a baul song from Kushtia, then American jazz. Her bookshelf is the same: poetry, physics, cookbooks and detective novels side by side. Her taste is eclectic: drawn from a wide variety of sources and styles. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to pick out, so an eclectic person selects the best from everywhere. Synonyms: diverse, wide-ranging.

gre.s: The architect's style resists easy categorization: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction, it is thoroughly ____.
gre.clue: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction

example: Nilufar's bookshelf is wonderfully eclectic, holding Bengali folk tales, Russian novels, cookbooks and a manual for repairing motorbikes.

en: Native to or regularly found in a particular place or group
hook: EN-DEMIC: IN the people (demos), always present there.
story: Endemic. Every monsoon, dengue fever returns to Dhaka. Doctors no longer treat it as a surprise; it is always present, rising and falling with the rains. Dengue is endemic in Bangladesh: regularly found in that place. The word also describes plants and animals native to one area, like the lemurs found only on Madagascar. Contrast it with epidemic, a sudden outbreak. En means in, and demos means people. Synonyms: native, prevalent, entrenched.

gre.s: Corruption was so ____ in the old regime that bribery was considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal.
gre.clue: considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal

example: Cheating was endemic at the exam centre, so the board sent outside invigilators and installed cameras in every hall.

en: Fair and impartial
hook: EQUITABLE: EQUAL for all.
story: Equitable. When their father died, three brothers in a Rajshahi village had to divide his mango orchard. The eldest wanted the biggest share. Their uncle walked the land, counted the trees, and drew the lines so that each brother received the same number of fruiting trees and equal access to the pond. Everyone agreed the division was equitable: fair and impartial. Equitable shares a root with equal and equity. Synonyms: fair, just, even-handed. Opposite: biased.

gre.s: Critics argued that the new tax was hardly ____, since it fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched.
gre.clue: fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched

example: The roommates worked out an equitable rota for washing dishes, based on how often each of them actually cooked.

en: To grow quickly worse, bigger or more serious
hook: ESCALATE: like an ESCALATOR, going up and up.
story: Escalate. It started with a small argument between two rickshaw pullers about who had the right of way. One shouted, and the other shouted louder. Passengers joined in, shopkeepers took sides, and within ten minutes a crowd of fifty was pushing and yelling. The argument had escalated: increased rapidly in intensity and seriousness. Think of an escalator, carrying you up step by step without stopping. Its opposite is de-escalate, to calm things down. Synonyms: intensify, mount, spiral.

gre.s: What began as a minor quarrel over a parking space threatened to ____ into a brawl as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides.
gre.clue: as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides

example: Prices at the cattle markets escalated sharply in the final days before Eid, as buyers rushed to find animals.

en: Perfectly clean and tidy; flawless
hook: IM-MACULATE: without a single spot (macula).
story: Immaculate. Before the hostel inspection, Ishita scrubbed the floor twice, folded every piece of clothing, arranged her books by height, and even polished the window bars. When the warden walked in, she ran a finger along the shelf and found not a speck of dust. The room was immaculate: perfectly clean and tidy. It can also mean flawless, as in an immaculate performance. In Latin, macula means spot or stain, so immaculate means spotless. Synonyms: spotless, pristine, flawless.

gre.s: Though the pianist had been ill all week, her performance was ____: critics who listened for even a single wrong note found none.
gre.clue: critics who listened for even a single wrong note found none

example: Even after a twelve-hour flight, the captain's white uniform looked immaculate as he walked through the terminal.

en: Cleverly inventive, especially in finding new ways to solve problems
hook: INGENIOUS: a GENIUS idea. Not to be confused with ingenuous (innocent).
story: Ingenious. When floods drowned the fields around villages in southern Bangladesh, farmers did not give up. They built floating gardens: rafts of water hyacinth layered with mud and compost, where vegetables grew while rising and falling with the water. Visiting scientists called the method ingenious: clever, original, and inventive. It shares a root with engine and genius. Do not confuse it with ingenuous, which means innocent and naive. Synonyms: inventive, resourceful, brilliant.

gre.s: The engineer's ____ design, which used ordinary bicycle parts to power a water pump, succeeded where expensive imported machines had repeatedly failed.
gre.clue: used ordinary bicycle parts to power a water pump

example: The ingenious puzzle box has no visible lock and opens only when its wooden panels are slid in a precise order.

en: A secret plot or scheme; to arouse curiosity
hook: INTRIGUE: the palace's secret plots that INTRIGUE you.
story: Intrigue. In the old Mughal courts, ministers whispered in dark corridors, bribed servants to read secret letters, and plotted to ruin their rivals. Historians call this palace intrigue: secret plotting and scheming. Lamia read about it in a historical novel and could not put the book down; the story intrigued her, arousing her curiosity until two in the morning. So as a noun, intrigue is a secret plot; as a verb, it means to fascinate. Synonyms: conspiracy, scheming; or, to fascinate.

gre.s: The royal court was rife with ____: ministers formed secret alliances, spread rumors about their rivals, and plotted against one another behind the king's back.
gre.clue: plotted against one another behind the king's back

example: The novel follows a young clerk caught up in the intrigue of a family firm, where cousins secretly plot to seize control.

en: Letting no light through; also, difficult to make sense of
hook: OPAQUE: light can't pass through; meaning can't pass through either.
story: Opaque. The bathroom window in Mitu's flat is made of frosted glass. Light comes in, but nobody can see through it. Opaque. Later that day, her economics professor explained monetary policy for an hour, using words nobody had heard before. At the end, not one student understood. His lecture was opaque too. Opaque means you cannot see through it, physically or intellectually. Its opposite is transparent or lucid.

gre.s: Critics complained that the company's accounting was deliberately ____, making it nearly impossible for investors to understand where the money went.
gre.clue: nearly impossible for investors to understand

example: The ministry's scholarship selection process remained opaque, and no applicant was ever told why they had been rejected.

en: Closely connected to the subject being discussed
hook: PERTINENT: PERTAINS to the topic.
story: Pertinent. In his job interview, Arif was asked about his teamwork skills. He resisted the urge to talk about his childhood or his love of cricket. Instead he gave three short examples, each directly related to the job's demands. The panel nodded approvingly. His answers were pertinent: directly relevant to the matter at hand. Pertinent pertains to the topic. Interestingly, impertinent once meant irrelevant, and now means rude.

gre.s: The judge excluded the testimony as not ____ to the case, since it concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime.
gre.clue: concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime

example: Before the vote, the councillor raised a pertinent question about who would pay to maintain the new park once it was built.

en: Present in every part of a place or group
hook: PERVASIVE: PERVADES everything, like a smell filling a house.
story: Pervasive. Farhan's mother fried onions for the evening's biryani. Within minutes, the smell had spread into every room, every curtain, every pillow, even the clothes in his cupboard. Two days later, his shirts still smelled of onions. The smell was pervasive: spreading widely throughout an area. Corruption can be pervasive too, seeping through every level of an organisation. Pervasive is close to ubiquitous. Think: it pervades everything.

gre.s: Researchers found the influence of social media so ____ that it shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives.
gre.clue: shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives

example: Fear of failure was so pervasive at the coaching centre that students hid their practice scores even from close friends.

en: To recommend a medicine; to state authoritatively what should be done
hook: PRE-SCRIBE: write (scribe) the rule BEFORE.
story: Prescribe. Ishita went to the clinic with a sore throat and a fever. The doctor examined her, then wrote on a slip of paper: an antibiotic, three times a day, for seven days. He had prescribed the medicine. Later, her hostel warden prescribed new rules: lights out by midnight, no guests after nine. To prescribe is to recommend a remedy, or to state with authority what must be done. Do not confuse proscribe, which means to forbid. Synonyms: dictate, stipulate.

gre.s: Unlike earlier grammarians, who sought to ____ rigid rules for correct usage, modern linguists aim merely to describe how people actually speak.
gre.clue: modern linguists aim merely to describe how people actually speak

example: School rules prescribe a white shirt and navy trousers, but many pupils add bright socks as a small act of rebellion.

en: To feel bitterness about unfair treatment
hook: RE-SENT: the insult is SENT back again and again in your mind.
story: Resent. For years, Imran's younger brother got the new clothes, the bigger room, and all the praise, while Imran did the chores. He never said a word, but he resented it deeply: he felt bitter about the unfair treatment. To resent is to feel bitterness or indignation at being treated unfairly. Resentment can simmer quietly for decades. Re means again, and sent comes from the Latin for feel: feeling a hurt again and again. Synonyms: begrudge, grudge.

gre.s: Veteran staff members tended to ____ the newcomers' rapid promotions, which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit.
gre.clue: which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit

example: Local fishermen resent the new trawlers from the city, which sweep up in one night what a small boat catches in a month.

en: Using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize people's foolishness
hook: SATIRICAL: SATIRE makes fun of the powerful.
story: Satirical. Every Friday night, a comedy show on TV portrays the country's politicians as cartoon characters fighting over a giant cake. One minister falls into the icing; another steals the cherry. The audience laughs. The politicians grumble. But behind the jokes is a serious point about greed. The show is satirical: using humour, irony, and exaggeration to criticize people's foolishness or vice. Satire has a serious message hidden behind the laughter.

gre.s: The magazine's ____ cartoons, which exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths, made him a laughingstock across the country.
gre.clue: exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths

example: Swift's satirical essay proposed that the poor of Ireland sell their babies as food, a shocking idea meant to expose official cruelty.

en: Thinly scattered; small in number or amount
hook: SPARSE: SPARE, very little.
story: Sparse. Nadia's grandfather was once very proud of his thick hair. But at seventy, it had become sparse: a few thin strands scattered across the top of his head. Sparse means thinly scattered, or small in number or amount. In a desert, vegetation is sparse. In remote char villages, doctors are sparse. Think of something lightly sprinkled across a wide space. Its opposite is dense or abundant. Synonyms: scanty, meagre, scattered.

gre.s: Attendance at the lecture was ____: barely a dozen listeners sat dotted across an auditorium built to hold five hundred.
gre.clue: barely a dozen listeners

example: Data on the rare river dolphins of the Sangu is sparse, so researchers rely partly on reports from local fishermen.

en: Showing simplicity and a lack of luxury; austere
hook: SPARTAN: like the warriors of SPARTA, tough and simple.
story: Spartan. The national cricket team's training camp in the hills was famously spartan: thin mattresses on concrete floors, cold showers at five in the morning, plain rice and lentils for every meal, and absolutely no phones. Some young players almost quit in the first week. By the end, they were tough, focused, and fitter than ever. Spartan means simple, plain, and lacking comfort. The ancient Spartans were famous for their harsh, disciplined lifestyle. Synonym: austere.

gre.s: The monks' ____ quarters contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle.
gre.clue: contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle

example: Mountaineers on the expedition lived a spartan life, melting snow for water and sleeping in thin tents at minus thirty.

en: Quiet and reflective, often slightly sad; soft and restrained
hook: SUBDUED: SUBjugated, toned down.
story: Subdued. Babu was usually the loudest person in the hostel, cracking jokes at every meal. But in the week after his grandmother died, he ate quietly, answered in single words, and spent his evenings reading alone. His friends noticed how subdued he was: quiet and reflective, a little sad. Subdued can also describe soft, restrained light or color, like the subdued lamps of a library. It comes from subdue, to bring under control. Synonyms: muted, restrained, low key, somber.

gre.s: In contrast to his usual exuberance, the comedian seemed oddly ____ throughout the interview, speaking softly and rarely smiling.
gre.clue: speaking softly and rarely smiling

example: After the heavy defeat, the usually noisy bus ride back to Sylhet was subdued, and most players slept or stared out of the windows.

en: Someone or something that takes the place of another
hook: SURROGATE: a SUBSTITUTE who stands in.
story: Surrogate. When Lamia's parents moved abroad for work, her aunt in Rajshahi raised her. She packed her lunch, attended parent meetings, and sat up with her through every fever. For ten years, her aunt was a surrogate mother: a substitute, someone acting in another's place. In medicine, a surrogate mother carries a baby for others. The word comes from the Latin for to elect in place of another. Synonyms: substitute, proxy, stand-in.

gre.s: Unable to attend the ceremony himself, the ailing laureate sent his daughter as a ____ to accept the award and read the speech he had written.
gre.clue: Unable to attend the ceremony himself

example: Keepers at some panda reserves wear panda costumes and act as surrogate mothers for cubs that are being prepared for the wild.

en: Passing quickly, not lasting long
hook: TRANSIENT: in TRANSIT, just passing through.
story: Transient. When Farhan failed his first university exam, the pain felt enormous. He skipped dinner and stared at the ceiling all night. A month later, after passing the retake, he could barely remember why he had been so upset. The pain had been transient: temporary, passing quickly. Hotels serve a transient population of travellers who never stay long. Think of people in transit. Synonyms: ephemeral, fleeting, evanescent.

gre.s: The economist argued that the price spike was ____, the result of a temporary shortage rather than a lasting change in demand.
gre.clue: a temporary shortage rather than a lasting change

example: The town's population is largely transient, since most residents are construction workers who move on once each project ends.

en: A formal written work dealing systematically with a subject
hook: TREATISE: a book that TREATS a subject thoroughly.
story: Treatise. Anika's grandfather spent twenty years writing a five-hundred-page book on the rice varieties of Bengal. It has chapters on soil, history, climate and cooking, each carefully argued, with tables and footnotes. Agricultural scholars still cite it today. It is a treatise: a formal written work dealing systematically with a subject. Do not confuse it with treaty, an agreement between nations. Kautilya's Arthashastra is a famous ancient treatise on statecraft. Synonyms: monograph, dissertation.

gre.s: Far from being a casual collection of anecdotes, the book is a rigorous ____, methodically working through every aspect of the philosopher's theory of justice.
gre.clue: methodically working through every aspect

example: In the eleventh century, Ibn Sina wrote a medical treatise so thorough that European universities taught from it for centuries.
